facts.statement: Fossil remains of Xenerodiops were discovered in Egypt by Elwyn L. Simons and formally described in 1987.
facts.quote: Its fossil remains were found in Egypt by Elwyn L. Simons and first formally described in 1987.

facts.statement: Xenerodiops lived during the Oligocene epoch, approximately 33 million years ago.
facts.quote: It lived in the Oligocene (about 33 million years ago).

facts.statement: Xenerodiops is classified in its own family, Xenerodiopidae, though some researchers argue this family is synonymous with the heron family Ardeidae.
facts.quote: It has been placed in its own family, Xenerodiopidae; the alternative view is that this family is synonymous with Ardeidae, the herons.

facts.statement: The stout humerus suggests that Xenerodiops had a robust physical structure.
facts.quote: The humerus was stout enough to suggests that this animal was of a robust structure.

facts.statement: The mobile rostrum suggests that Xenerodiops was capable of delivering a powerful bite.
facts.quote: The rostrum was very mobile and it seems that the animal was able to exercise a powerful bite.

facts.statement: Fossils of Xenerodiops have been found in Egypt, though it may also be present in Libya.
facts.quote: Xenerodiops mycter was found in Egypt, but may be the same species as one found in Libya.

facts.statement: The genus name Xenerodiops is derived from Greek words meaning 'stranger heron resemblance'.
facts.quote: The genus name is formed from the Greek xenos, stranger, erodios, heron, and ops, here meaning resemblance.

facts.statement: The species name mycter comes from the Greek word for 'nose'.
facts.quote: The species name mycter is from the Greek mykter, nose.

facts.statement: When described, herons were classified in the order Ciconiiformes, which has since been split and now places herons in Pelecaniformes.
facts.quote: At the time, herons were placed in the order Ciconiiformes, known to be paraphyletic. The order has since been split, with herons placed in Pelecaniformes.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Xenerodiops mycter and Zeltornis ginsburgi are the same species, as they were described from different fossil parts.
facts.quote: Jiří Mlíkovský compared X. mycter with Zeltornis ginsburgi, found in Miocene deposits in Libya. He considered that they might be the same species, although this could not be settled as they were described from different fossilized parts.

facts.statement: Some researchers have synonymized the family Xenerodiopidae with Ardeidae because the beak shape resembles that of the Nycticoracinae subfamily.
facts.quote: However, he did synonymize the family Xenerodiopidae with Ardeidae, partly on the grounds that the unusually shaped rostrum was similar to those of other members of the subfamily Nycticoracinae.

facts.statement: The time range for Xenerodiops is estimated to be between 33.9 and 27.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Rupelian to Rupelian (33.9 to 27.3 million years ago)
